title: BFM-Zero: Promptable Humanoid Control from One Shared World
one_liner: One shared latent space lets a single policy control a real humanoid robot on any task without retraining.
lead: A humanoid robot can do many tasks: walk to a goal, copy a motion, respond to a reward signal. Normally, each task needs its own specialized policy. BFM-Zero learns one shared latent space (a common language) where motions, goals, and rewards all live together. This lets a single policy handle all three kinds of tasks without any retraining, and even learn new ones with just a few examples.

paras: A humanoid robot is like a musician who can play many songs. Today, we train a separate expert policy (a set of rules and weights) for each task: one policy copies motions, another reaches goals, a third responds to reward signals. When a new task appears, we retrain from scratch.

The naive fix would be to train one giant policy on all tasks at once. This usually fails because the tasks pull the learning in different directions—the policy learns to do none of them well. A policy optimized for motion tracking learns to track, not to reach goals. The two objectives clash.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Learn one shared latent space where motions, goals, and rewards all speak the same language, so one policy can prompt any task without retraining.

paras: The paper moves from training separate policies to training one latent space that speaks all task languages at once. The single policy never changes; only what you feed it (the prompt in latent space) changes.

hidden.name: Latent alignment across task domains
paras: A latent space is an invisible map where similar things cluster near each other. Here, a motion that reaches a goal sits close to the goal state itself—they share coordinates. Rewards that reinforce similar motions sit nearby too.

The paper measures this alignment by training a forward-backward model (predict what comes next, predict what came before) on unlabeled robot data. If the space aligns motions and goals, a single policy can learn to read it. The paper validates this by checking if one policy can handle all three task types without task-specific retraining.

heat.caption: Darker means more alignment to task semantics. Highlights show task-relevant coordinates.

reads.html: The latent space is a coordinate system where all tasks fit. A motion trajectory becomes a vector (a list of numbers). A goal state becomes a vector in the same space. A reward signal becomes a vector there too. One policy can read any of them because they speak the same language.

The latent space is induced by an unsupervised forward-backward model objective. Forward-backward models learn smooth, objective-centric representations of trajectories that generalize across different reward functions and goal specifications, naturally aligning motions and task semantics.

mechanism.h2: Why one space works where three policies don't
paras: Three separate policies pull learning in three directions and interfere. One shared space avoids that interference because all tasks speak the same language from the start.

The forward-backward model (unsupervised pretraining) builds a smooth map where nearby points in latent space represent similar behaviors. This map is task-agnostic—it learns motion structure without needing labels. Once that map exists, a single policy can learn to read it and route any prompt (motion, goal, reward) to the right action. A new task just adds a new prompt; it does not re-shuffle the space.

Domain randomization (changing physics parameters randomly during training) and asymmetric learning (stronger updates on certain motion types) help bridge the gap between simulation and real robot hardware, because when training sees many different physics setups, the learned policy becomes reliable against the real physics it will face. Reward shaping guides exploration toward useful behaviors early on by steering the learning toward regions of latent space that correspond to real, useful motions. Together, these prevent the one policy from overfitting to one task or getting stuck in poor local solutions, because it learns to navigate the whole latent space, not just one corner of it.

stages.s: Motion trajectory, goal state, or reward signal
Encode into latent space using forward-backward model
Robot executes motion, reaches goal, or follows reward

math.words: Loss = forward reconstruction error + backward reconstruction error + policy adaptation cost. Forward predicts the next state. Backward predicts the past state. Both forces the latent space to capture motion structure. Policy adapts to new prompts with small gradient steps in latent space.
symbols: latent vector at time t (the coordinates in the shared space)
robot state (joint positions and velocities) at time t
forward model that predicts next state from latent code
backward model that predicts past state from latent code
policy that takes latent prompt z and outputs robot action
loss for the current task (tracking, reaching, or reward)
weight controlling how easy the policy is to adapt (small lambda means easy zero-shot)

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose a motion trajectory gets encoded into latent vector z = [3.2, -1.5, 0.8].
Forward model predicts next state: ||true_s_next - predicted_s_next||^2 = 0.09. Large error means z does not capture the motion well.
Backward model predicts prior state: ||true_s_prev - predicted_s_prev||^2 = 0.04. Both errors add: 0.09 + 0.04 = 0.13.
Policy adaptation on a new task: gradient step on z costs lambda * 0.002 = 0.0002 (if lambda is 0.1). Small cost means the policy can easily specialize to the new task using just the latent prompt.

math.note: The forward and backward models squeeze all task structure into latent space; the policy just learns to read prompts from that space.

charts.title: Three separate policies
charts.note: Each policy is specialized but needs retraining for every new task.

charts.title: One shared policy (BFM-Zero)
charts.note: Slightly lower per-task accuracy (shared space forces compromise) but handles new tasks instantly and uses fewer weights.

items.html: If the forward-backward pretraining is weak, the latent space may encode motions poorly, and the policy cannot read them correctly. The fix is longer unsupervised pretraining or better forward-backward objectives, because more training time or clearer supervision signals force the forward and backward models to actually learn the structure of motion, rather than letting them cheat by ignoring parts of the trajectory.

If you train the policy too hard on motion tracking, it forgets how to reach goals. The fix is balanced training (sample tasks evenly) and gentle steering (small nudges to keep the policy from specializing too narrowly).

A latent space learned in simulation may not work on a real robot because real physics have friction, cable stretch, and sensor noise that simulation does not capture. Domain randomization and asymmetric learning help mitigate this by exposing the learning to varied conditions, but some tasks may still fail in the real world if the gap between simulated and real physics is too wide to bridge with just randomization.

A new task may require a latent prompt from a region of space the policy never trained on. If the policy never visited that corner of the space, few-shot learning may get stuck in a bad local solution because it has no good weight values in that region to start from. The fix is better initialization (start closer to good solutions) or broader latent space coverage during pretraining (explore more of the map), because then the policy has seen many regions and can gracefully adapt to any new prompt.

Strong unsupervised pretraining builds a smooth, well-aligned latent space because forward-backward models learn the true structure of motions. Balanced multi-task training keeps the policy general because it avoids specializing to any one task. Domain randomization closes the sim-to-real gap because the policy learns invariances to physics variation. Few-shot optimization then enables rapid specialization to unseen tasks because the policy has already learned the latent space layout and just needs to adjust its reading head.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Simulate a humanoid robot in a physics engine (e.g., MuJoCo). Train a forward-backward model on unlabeled motion data. Encode three task prompts (a recorded motion trajectory, a goal position, a reward trajectory) into the latent space. Train one policy on a mix of all three tasks. Then test: feed the policy a new task prompt from a held-out test set (a motion it never trained on, a goal it never saw, a reward signal it never experienced). Measure: does the policy complete the task zero-shot, or does it need just a few adaptation steps?
demo.metric_eq: Zero_shot_success = 1 if policy completes task without fine-tuning, 0 otherwise. Few_shot_steps = number of gradient updates needed to adapt to a new task in latent space.
demo.closing: The core thing to see: one policy reading a learned latent prompt beats training three separate policies. Zero-shot should work on at least 70% of new tasks.
